summary: This standards-track RFC specifies version 3 of the RPCSEC_GSS Remote Procedure Call security protocol. It supports multi-principal authentication, security label assertions, structured privilege assertions and channel bindings. It updates RFC 5403.

plainLanguage.summary: The security guard for remote program calls gets new skills, such as checking several identities at once and attaching labels.

questions: how does multi-principal authentication work in rpc
what is the rpcsec_gss child handle
subtitle: Version 3 of the RPC security layer lets a client bind extra claims, such as a second identity, labels or privileges, to a session.

tldr.problem: Existing GSS-API mechanisms cannot tell a server certain authorization and authentication facts, such as a security label for a process, a privilege for a copy, or the user behind a trusted client host.
tldr.mechanism: RPCSEC_GSSv3 adds two control procedures, RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE and RPCSEC_GSS_LIST. A client uses an existing (parent) handle to ask the server for a new (child) handle that carries multi-principal authentication, a channel binding, label assertions or structured privilege assertions.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5403. It is a superset of versions 1 and 2, so it should be used when the new functionality is needed.

facts.label: Assertion kinds
facts.value: Multi-principal, channel binding, label, structured privilege

today: RFC 7861 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016. It updates RFC 5403, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Third Version
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSS protects remote procedure calls (RPC) using the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API). The original protocol, RFC 2203, authenticated RPC clients and servers to each other. The second version, RFC 5403, added support for channel bindings.

The RFC says existing GSS-API mechanisms are insufficient for conveying some authorization and authentication information to a server. It solves this at the application layer, in RPCSEC_GSS itself, instead of extending GSS-API. A major motivation is multi-level (labeled) security and server-side copy for NFSv4, described in RFC 7862.

Multi-principal authentication also addresses shared cache poisoning. On a machine with several users and one cache manager, data fetched under the first user's credentials could be re-displayed to others, so a malicious user might slip bogus data into the cache.
sections.plainLanguage: The old guard could check who you are, but could not take extra notes about you. Some programs needed those notes, so a new version was made.

sections.title: Parent Handles, Child Handles and Versions
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSSv3 is very similar to version 2, and the RFC shows only the differences. A client first uses an existing context handle, set up in the usual way, as the parent handle to protect its exchanges. The server answers an RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE request with a child handle, which uses the same underlying GSS-API security context as the parent. A child handle MUST NOT be used as the parent in a later create message, and child handles MUST be destroyed when their parent is destroyed.

To use the new version, an initiator sends a request with rgc_version set to RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_3 (the value 3). If the target does not recognize it, the target returns an RPC error. An initiator MUST NOT use a handle from version 3 with version 1 or 2 of the same target, or the reverse.

Everything in version 2 still works except the RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL operation. A server that receives it on a version 3 handle MUST answer MSG_ACCEPTED with PROC_UNAVAIL. Channel binding is done differently in version 3.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your ID once and get a main pass. Then you can ask for extra passes, each tied to the main one, that say more about you. If the main pass is thrown away, so are the extras.

sections.title: The New Reply Verifier
sections.content:
A child handle shares a GSS context with its parent, so a child and a parent could end up with the same RPCSEC_GSS sequence numbers. Earlier versions compute the reply verifier, a Message Integrity Code (MIC), over only the sequence number, which gives a man-in-the-middle attacker an opening.

Version 3 fixes this by computing the reply verifier from exactly the same input as the request verifier, except that mtype is REPLY instead of CALL. The MIC covers xid, mtype, rpcvers, prog, vers, proc and the cred, which binds the RPCSEC_GSS handle.
sections.plainLanguage: If two passes could carry the same number, a trickster might swap replies. So the stamp on each reply now covers much more than the number, including which pass it belongs to.

sections.title: The Two New Control Procedures
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE binds any combination of assertions (multi-principal authentication, labels, structured privileges or channel bindings) to a new context returned in the rcr_handle field of rgss3_create_res. RPCSEC_GSS_LIST asks the target which assertions it supports. Both are control messages and look like a data message to NULLPROC. The client MUST protect them with rpc_gss_svc_integrity or rpc_gss_svc_privacy, and MUST NOT use rpc_gss_svc_none.

The request carries rgss3_create_args: an optional multi-principal block, an optional channel-binding MIC and a list of assertions. The reply lists the assertions that succeeded, in the same order as the request. A server MAY map labels, privileges and identities to local values according to its policy.

For channel binding, the client prefixes the channel-bindings data with the channel type from RFC 5056, takes a MIC of it using the parent's GSS-API context and puts it in rca_chan_bind_mic. A server that supports the feature MUST verify it and reply with its own MIC. If the client cannot verify the reply, it MUST call RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY. If the server returns no binding, the client MAY carry on, unless it considers channel binding critical, in which case it MUST destroy the handle.

A child handle bound to a secure channel SHOULD be used only with rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two new questions you can ask the guard: 'please make me a special pass with these notes attached' and 'what kinds of notes do you accept?'. Both must be sent in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Multi-Principal Authentication
sections.content:
A client MAY assert two identities at once: the RPC client host and a user. This helps when a server will grant authority only to a user acting through a trusted host. It will refuse the user alone, such as an unprivileged user-space program, and the host alone.

The parent handle MUST correspond to a GSS-API context that authenticates the client host. The inner handle, in rgmp_handle, MUST authenticate the user. The reverse MUST NOT be used. The client also places a MIC of the RPC header in rgmp_rpcheader_mic, computed with the inner handle's context. The create call MUST use the rpc_gss_svc_privacy service, which prevents an attacker from reassigning the parent handle and stealing the user's identity.

The server checks that the parent is a client host context, then verifies the MIC. On success it returns the inner handle plus a MIC over the reply header, and treats the child handle as authenticating the user principal. A missing parent context gives RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM. A missing inner context, or a MIC that does not verify, gives the new RPCSEC_GSS_INNER_CREDPROBLEM.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the guard will only let a student into the lab if the student shows up together with a trusted teacher. This is how both show their IDs at the same time.

sections.title: Label and Privilege Assertions
sections.content:
A label assertion (rgss3_label) carries a Label Format Specifier (rgss3_lfs, with an LFS id and a policy identifier) and an opaque label. It lets an NFS client process assert its security label so the server can enforce Full Mode mandatory access control against file labels. A client finds supported formats with RPCSEC_GSS_LIST. If a label needs secrecy, the client MUST use rpc_gss_svc_privacy. A server without labeling, or without the requested format, rejects with RPCSEC_GSS_LABEL_PROBLEM.

A structured privilege (rgss3_privs) is a capability defined by an RPC application, with a name in rp_name and opaque application data in rp_privilege. RPCSEC_GSSv3 only passes the data along. A server that does not recognize an assertion rejects with RPCSEC_GSS_UNKNOWN_MESSAGE. If a request contains unsupported privileges the answer is RPCSEC_GSS_PRIVILEGE_PROBLEM. The server MUST NOT reject a request containing supported assertions merely because some of them were refused, for example by local policy. RFC 7862 uses this for inter-server copy.

New assertion types can be added later as new arms of the rgss3_assertion_u union. There is no create payload that every implementation is required to support: implementations are feature driven.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is like a colored wristband that says what rooms you may enter. A privilege is a permission slip made by one particular program. The guard just passes them along and lets the program decide.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Assertions are claims by the client, so the server must weigh them against whether the client and user are authenticated, whether multi-principal authentication was used, whether the client is trusted and what server policy allows. What an assertion means is specific to the application protocol.

RPCSEC_GSSv3 is not a complete labeling solution: it conveys the labels of actors, not of objects. The RFC also warns about NFSv4 callbacks. In NFSv4.1 the server SHOULD choose RPCSEC_GSS handles that authenticate the client when protecting callbacks related to state created under version 3 contexts. The new reply verifier addresses the man-in-the-middle attacks described for SSV in RFC 5661.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard should not believe every note blindly. He checks who handed it over and what the rules say before he lets anyone in.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Four new RPC authentication status numbers were added: RPCSEC_GSS_INNER_CREDPROBLEM (15), RPCSEC_GSS_LABEL_PROBLEM (16), RPCSEC_GSS_PRIVILEGE_PROBLEM (17) and RPCSEC_GSS_UNKNOWN_MESSAGE (18).

IANA also created the RPCSEC_GSS Structured Privilege Names Registry, managed under Standards Action. Names must be 1 to 128 UTF-8 characters, the prefix EXPE is reserved for experiments and PRIV is for private use. The initial entries are copy_to_auth, copy_from_auth and copy_confirm_auth from RFC 7862.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers and names for the new error codes and permission slips are written down in an official list so everyone uses them the same way.
